## Chain Convergence {#sec-convergence}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 2.B.
:::

For the reference fit: divergent transitions **`r n_div`**, iterations at
maximum treedepth **`r n_tree`**, largest $\hat R$ over all
`r nrow(sm_ref)` estimated parameters **`r fmt(max(sm_ref$rhat), 4)`**.

The conclusions rest on more than the reference fit: the intercept-only
model supplies the Q1 comparison and the prior variants supply the sensitivity
analysis. The same diagnostics therefore appear for all eleven runs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diag-all
mf$diagnostics |>
  transmute(Fit = fit, `parameters` = n_par, `max Rhat` = max_rhat,
            `min bulk ESS` = round(min_ess_bulk),
            `min tail ESS` = round(min_ess_tail),
            `divergent transitions` = divergent,
            `at max treedepth` = max_treedepth) |>
  kt(caption = sprintf("Diagnostics for all eleven runs, each of %s post-warmup draws.",
                       format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")), digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: div-readout
#| echo: false
d_any <- mf$diagnostics |> filter(divergent > 0)
```

`r if (nrow(d_any) == 0) "No run produced a divergent transition." else sprintf("%d of the eleven runs produced a small number of divergent transitions (%s) against %s draws each, which is at most %s%% of the transitions in any run. Two observations bear on how much weight to put on them: the affected runs' Rhat and ESS are indistinguishable from the clean ones, and their posteriors coincide with the reference in @fig-sens-icc. The usual explanation for divergences at this rate in a hierarchical model with 26 clusters and a 7 x 7 correlation matrix is mild curvature in the posterior near zero variance, but this report has not located them in parameter space and so offers that as an inference rather than as a demonstration. All eleven runs are reported here in full.", nrow(d_any), paste(sprintf("%s: %d", d_any$fit, d_any$divergent), collapse = ", "), format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ","), fmt(100 * max(d_any$divergent) / mf$ndraws, 3))`

@tbl-diag-all reduces each run to its worst value on each diagnostic, which is
the right summary for deciding whether a run is usable and the wrong one for
seeing how the chains behaved. @fig-mcmc-rank shows the chains themselves for
the reference fit. It uses rank plots rather than trace plots, on the argument
of Vehtari, Gelman, Simpson, et al. (2021), who introduced the $\hat R$ this
report quotes and proposed the rank plot alongside it: with
`r format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")` draws a trace plot is an unreadable band
of ink, whereas ranking the draws across chains and counting each chain's
share of each rank bin stays legible at any chain length and exposes chains
that differ in location or in scale.

```{r}
#| label: rank-prep
#| echo: false
NBIN  <- 20L
nchn  <- length(unique(dr_ref$.chain))
ndrw  <- nrow(dr_ref)

icc_mat <- vapply(resps, function(r) icc_draws(dr_ref, r, resp_fam[[r]]),
                  numeric(ndrw))
colnames(icc_mat) <- paste0("ICC: ", rlab(resps))
sel      <- unique(c(sm_ref$variable[which.min(sm_ref$ess_bulk)],
                     sm_ref$variable[which.min(sm_ref$ess_tail)], "lp__"))
par_mat  <- vapply(sel, function(v) as.numeric(dr_ref[[v]]), numeric(ndrw))
rank_mat <- cbind(icc_mat, par_mat)

rank_long <- bind_rows(lapply(colnames(rank_mat), function(v) {
  rk <- rank(rank_mat[, v], ties.method = "random")
  data.frame(Quantity = v, chain = factor(dr_ref$.chain),
             bin = ceiling(rk / (ndrw / NBIN)))
})) |>
  count(Quantity, chain, bin) |>
  mutate(Quantity = factor(Quantity, levels = colnames(rank_mat)))

rank_ncol <- ceiling(sqrt(ncol(rank_mat)))
```

The `r ncol(rank_mat)` quantities in the figure are chosen by a rule fixed in
the code rather than by inspection. The seven ICCs are there because Q1 rests
on them and because the smallest effective sample size anywhere in the
analysis is one of them (@sec-resolution). The rest are the sampled parameter
with the lowest bulk ESS, the sampled parameter with the lowest tail ESS, and
the log posterior density, which come to `r length(sel)` panels because
`r if (length(sel) < 3) "one parameter is worst on both counts" else "the three are distinct"`.
A reader expecting the figure to reveal a problem will be disappointed, which
is its purpose: with $\hat R$ at `r fmt(max(sm_ref$rhat), 4)` and `r n_div`
divergent transitions the chains should look interchangeable, and the figure
lets a reader confirm that instead of taking the summary on trust.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mcmc-rank
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "Rank plots for the reference fit. The draws of each quantity are pooled across the four chains and ranked; each line counts how many of one chain's draws fall in each of 20 equal rank bins. Under convergence every chain contributes an equal share of every bin, so the four lines should be flat and overlapping around the dashed expected count. A chain running high at one end of the axis and low at the other has explored a different part of the distribution from the others. The seven ICCs are derived draw by draw and diagnosed exactly like sampled parameters; the remaining panels are the log posterior density and the sampled parameters with the lowest bulk and tail effective sample sizes."
ggplot(rank_long, aes(bin, n, colour = chain)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ndrw / (NBIN * nchn), linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.3, colour = GREY) +
  geom_step(direction = "mid", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ Quantity, ncol = rank_ncol,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 24)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL[seq_len(nchn)], name = "chain") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, NBIN / 2, NBIN)) +
  labs(x = sprintf("rank of the draw among all %s, in %d equal bins",
                   format(ndrw, big.mark = ","), NBIN),
       y = "draws per chain") +
  fig_theme +
  theme(legend.title = element_text(size = 8.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-convergence
#| fig-cap: "Rhat (A) and bulk effective sample size (B) for every estimated parameter, and for the seven ICCs, which are derived quantities computed draw by draw and diagnosed like any other."
SHOW("convergence.png")
```

## Chain Resolution {#sec-resolution}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 2.C.
:::

Kruschke (2021) suggests an ESS of about 10,000, with the explicit
qualification that the figure aims at the stability of HDI limits and that
quantile-based limits are less demanding. This report is quantile-based
throughout (@sec-posterior-summary), so it gives both: the ESS, and the Monte
Carlo standard error of each quantile it reports.

```{r}
#| label: conv-prep
#| echo: false
full_tbl <- bind_rows(
  bind_rows(lapply(sm_ref$variable, function(v) {
    x <- dr_ref[[v]]; s <- draw_summary(x)
    d <- sm_ref[sm_ref$variable == v, ]
    data.frame(Parameter = v, s, rhat = d$rhat,
               ess_bulk = d$ess_bulk, ess_tail = d$ess_tail)
  })),
  icc_ref |> transmute(Parameter = paste0("ICC_", Response), Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi,
                       Mode, HDI_lo, HDI_hi, MCSE_lo, MCSE_med, MCSE_hi, SD,
                       rhat, ess_bulk, ess_tail))

is_offset <- startsWith(full_tbl$Parameter, "r_Locality__")
is_cor    <- startsWith(full_tbl$Parameter, "cor_Locality__")
shown_tbl <- full_tbl[!is_offset & !is_cor, ]
```

The table below prints the `r nrow(shown_tbl)` quantities this report quotes
or discusses. The `r nrow(full_tbl)` quantities of the full model also include
`r sum(is_offset)` locality offsets and `r sum(is_cor)` locality-intercept
correlations, which @fig-caterpillar and @tbl-cor already give; printing them
again here would bury the rows a reader needs in a table of
`r nrow(full_tbl)`. The summaries below the table are computed over all
`r nrow(full_tbl)`, and the archive contains the complete version.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence and resolution for the slopes, the intercepts, the auxiliary parameters and the locality SDs, and for the seven derived ICCs. Median and equal-tailed limits are given with their Monte Carlo standard errors; mode and HDI limits are given alongside, following the reference BARG document. The locality offsets and the locality-intercept correlations are left out of the printed table: @fig-caterpillar draws the offsets, @tbl-cor gives the correlations with their own diagnostics, and the complete table is deposited with the archive (@sec-reproducibility)."
shown_tbl |>
  transmute(Parameter,
            `median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `mode` = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `MCSE 2.5%` = MCSE_lo, `MCSE median` = MCSE_med, `MCSE 97.5%` = MCSE_hi,
            `Rhat` = rhat, `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk), `ESS tail` = round(ess_tail)) |>
  kt(caption = NULL, digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: ess-summary
#| echo: false
min_bulk <- min(full_tbl$ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE)
min_tail <- min(full_tbl$ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE)
worst    <- full_tbl$Parameter[which.min(full_tbl$ess_bulk)]
rel_all  <- with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD)
rel_all  <- rel_all[is.finite(rel_all)]
mcse_rel <- max(rel_all)
mcse_par <- full_tbl$Parameter[which.max(replace(with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD),
                                                 !is.finite(with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD)), -Inf))]
n_below_10k <- sum(full_tbl$ess_bulk < 10000, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Smallest bulk ESS: **`r format(round(min_bulk), big.mark = ",")`**
(`r worst`); smallest tail ESS:
**`r format(round(min_tail), big.mark = ",")`**.
`r n_below_10k` of the `r nrow(full_tbl)` quantities have a bulk ESS below
Kruschke's 10,000, so the recommendation is not met everywhere even at
`r format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")` draws. What matters for a
quantile-based report is the Monte Carlo error of the quantiles themselves.
The largest MCSE of a reported median, as a fraction of that parameter's own
posterior SD, is **`r fmt(mcse_rel, 4)`** (`r mcse_par`), so the simulation
noise in the numbers this report quotes is about
**`r format(round(1 / mcse_rel), big.mark = ",")` times smaller** than the
posterior uncertainty it describes. @tbl-convergence gives the per-parameter
MCSEs for anyone who wants to check a particular one.

## How Many Digits the Simulation Supports {#sec-digits}

Gelman, Vehtari, McElreath, et al. (2026, sec. 11.6) argue that the number of
digits to report should follow from the Monte Carlo error and the posterior
uncertainty rather than from a printing default, and they take two significant
digits as the usual answer. Since the previous section has already computed
the Monte Carlo standard error of every quantile this report quotes, the rule
can be applied to this document rather than merely cited.

```{r}
#| label: digits-audit
#| echo: false
dig <- full_tbl |>
  filter(is.finite(MCSE_med), MCSE_med > 0, is.finite(SD), SD > 0) |>
  mutate(
    d_mcse = floor(-log10(2 * MCSE_med)),
    d_post = floor(-log10(SD)) + 2)
d_min   <- min(dig$d_mcse)
d_med   <- median(dig$d_mcse)
n_bound <- sum(dig$d_post > dig$d_mcse)
n_free  <- sum(dig$d_post <= dig$d_mcse)
n_over3 <- sum(dig$d_mcse < 3)
```

Each of the `r nrow(dig)` quantities in the model has two ceilings. The
simulation supports decimal places up to the point where the Monte Carlo
standard error stays below half a unit in the last digit. The posterior
supports decimal places up to two significant digits of its own standard
deviation, beyond which further digits describe the width of a distribution
the data have not resolved that finely. Across the `r nrow(dig)` quantities the
first ceiling runs from `r d_min` to `r max(dig$d_mcse)` decimal places with a
median of `r d_med`; it is the binding one for `r n_bound` quantities, and the
posterior's own width binds first for the other `r n_free`.

The audit is unflattering to the tables. They print three decimal places by
default and four in @tbl-convergence, while `r n_over3` of the `r nrow(dig)`
quantities support fewer than three. Trimming a shared `digits` argument would
not fix it, because the ceiling varies from `r d_min` to
`r max(dig$d_mcse)` across rows measured on three different link scales, so no
single setting is right for all of them. The per-row answer is already in the
table: the three MCSE columns beside every quantile say how far that row can
be read, and they are printed for this reason. A reader comparing two numbers
that differ only in the third decimal place should look at that row's MCSE
before treating the difference as real.

Where a single figure has to be chosen, two decimal places is what the rule
endorses for a typical quantity here, and it is what the summaries in
@sec-summary and @tbl-sens-full use. Buying one further digit would mean
halving the Monte Carlo error, which needs four times the iterations.

## What This Report Does Not Check: Calibration {#sec-sbc}

Convergence diagnostics establish that the sampler explored the posterior of
the model that was coded. They cannot establish that the coded model is the
one intended, nor that the posterior it returns is calibrated. Simulation-based
calibration checking (Modrák, Moon, Kim, et al. 2025) is the tool for that: draw
parameters from the prior, simulate a dataset from them, refit, and check that
the rank of each drawn parameter within its own posterior is uniform across
many repetitions. This report does not perform it, and the honest account has
two parts, of which only the second is a real defence.

The first part is cost, and it is a weaker excuse than it looks. One fit of
this model takes about `r fmt(median(mf$minutes, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` minutes on
the machine that produced this document, taking the median over the eleven
runs (@sec-reproducibility), so the few hundred refits a calibration check needs
come to roughly
`r fmt(median(mf$minutes, na.rm = TRUE) * 300 / (60 * 24), 1)` days of
continuous computation, and less than that in parallel. That is affordable.
Gelman, Vehtari, McElreath, et al. (2026, sec. 14.3) add that a handful of
replications beats none, because ranks at the extremes of the range reveal
gross problems even in small numbers. Cost alone therefore does not justify
omitting the check.

The second part is specific to this model.
Calibration checking draws its parameters from the prior, so it checks the
model where the prior puts its mass. The intercept priors here are
deliberately wide, spanning 6 to 100 mm of thickness and 26 to 104 degrees of
edge angle before the data are seen (@tbl-intercept-prior), which
is what @sec-prior-pred asks of them. Datasets simulated from those priors
would include assemblages no lithic analyst would recognise, and calibration
verified over that range says little about the much narrower region the
posterior actually occupies. Gelman, Vehtari, McElreath, et al. (2026, sec.
14.3) identify exactly this tension between weakly informative priors and
calibration checking, and point to posterior SBC (Säilynoja, Schmitt, Bürkner
and Vehtari 2026), which conditions the simulation on the observed data and so
checks calibration where the answers live. They recommend it in particular for
assessing the size of any bias when convergence diagnostics show only faint
signs of trouble, which is the position of the
`r sum(mf$diagnostics$divergent > 0)` runs in @tbl-diag-all with a handful of
divergent transitions.

Posterior SBC on the reference fit is therefore the computational check this
analysis most clearly still owes, and a reader should treat the evidence in
this appendix as evidence about the sampler rather than about the calibration
of the model.

## The Checks That Were Specified in Advance {#sec-ppc-stats}

```{r}

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppc-stats
ppc_stat_tbl |>
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response),
         inside = observed >= rep_lo & observed <= rep_hi,
         verdict = ifelse(inside, "reproduced", "NOT reproduced")) |>
  transmute(Response, Statistic, observed,
            `replicated median` = rep_median, `2.5%` = rep_lo, `97.5%` = rep_hi,
            verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Observed test statistics against their posterior predictive distributions.")
```

```{r}
#| label: ppc-readout
#| echo: false
gs <- function(r, s) ppc_stat_tbl[ppc_stat_tbl$Response == r & ppc_stat_tbl$Statistic == s, ]
rg_neg <- gs("RG", "share below zero"); rg_min <- gs("RG", "minimum")
gi_one <- gs("GIUR", "share exactly 1"); rl_one <- gs("RLI", "share exactly 1")
ns_disp <- gs("NScar", "variance / mean")
```

### Does the Gaussian Likelihood for Retouch Generations Predict Negative Values?

The observed share of retouch-generation values below zero is
`r fmt(rg_neg$observed, 3)`; over the replicated datasets the share has median
`r fmt(rg_neg$rep_median, 3)` and 95% interval
[`r fmt(rg_neg$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(rg_neg$rep_hi, 3)`]. The observed minimum
is `r fmt(rg_min$observed, 2)` against a replicated interval of
[`r fmt(rg_min$rep_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(rg_min$rep_hi, 2)`]. The gaussian's
support extends below zero, while the fitted mean sits far enough above it
relative to the residual SD that the model rarely generates impossible values
in practice. The gaussian misses the *discreteness* instead: retouch
generations are recorded as a small number of counted generations averaged
over at most three edges, so the observed distribution is a spike train and
the replicated one is smooth. @fig-post-pred shows it, and it is a real
limitation of the family, though it leaves a location parameter unbiased.

The check is a judgement call rather than a pass or a failure, so the
`ref_rg_ln` fit refits the same response as a lognormal for comparison
(@sec-model-series), letting a reader see directly whether the choice of
family moves the conclusions:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rg-alt
ls_ln  <- sd(log(mod_dat$RG))
dr_ln  <- local({ f <- gf("ref_rg_ln"); d <- as_draws_df(f); rm(f); gc(); d })
rg_alt <- bind_rows(lapply(preds, function(pp) {
  x <- dr_ln[[paste0("b_RG_", pp)]] / ls_ln
  q <- eti(x); p <- 100 * mean(abs(x) < ROPE_SD)
  data.frame(Family = "lognormal (comparison)", Predictor = plab(pp),
             `standardised median` = median(x), `2.5%` = q[1], `97.5%` = q[2],
             `% in ROPE` = p,
             Verdict = rope_verdict(q[1], q[2], p, ROPE_SD),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
bind_rows(
  cf |> filter(Response == "RG") |>
    transmute(Family = "gaussian (reference)", Predictor = plab(Predictor),
              `standardised median` = Std_median,
              `2.5%` = Std_lo, `97.5%` = Std_hi,
              `% in ROPE` = pct_in_ROPE, Verdict),
  rg_alt) |>
  arrange(Predictor, Family) |>
  kt(caption = "Retouch generations: the reference gaussian fit against a lognormal refit of the same response. Both are shown on their own standardised axis, so the ROPE is +/- 0.1 in each case.")
```

### Do the Zero-One-Inflated Beta Fits Reproduce the Pile-Up at 1?

For GIUR the observed share of exact ones is `r fmt(gi_one$observed, 3)`
against a replicated interval of
[`r fmt(gi_one$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(gi_one$rep_hi, 3)`]; for the retouched
perimeter, `r fmt(rl_one$observed, 3)` against
[`r fmt(rl_one$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(rl_one$rep_hi, 3)`]. The share of exact
zeros is 0 in the data and 0 in the replications. That agreement shows only
that the zero-inflation half of the family is estimating a probability the
data have pinned at essentially zero, and says nothing about whether the model
captures zero inflation. See the note in @sec-likelihood.

### Is the Overdispersion of the Scar Count Captured?

The observed variance-to-mean ratio is `r fmt(ns_disp$observed, 2)`, well
above the value of 1 a Poisson would imply; the replicated interval is
[`r fmt(ns_disp$rep_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(ns_disp$rep_hi, 2)`]. The negative
binomial captures it.

# Appendix E. Full Posterior Summaries {#sec-posterior-summary}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 3.B.
:::

::: {.barg}
Every interval in this report is a 95% equal-tailed (percentile) credible
interval, running from the 2.5th to the 97.5th posterior percentile, and every
point summary in the text is the posterior median. That is the quantile-based
convention. The density-based pair, the posterior mode and the 95%
highest-density interval, appears alongside it in @tbl-convergence and
@tbl-coef-full, following the reference BARG document, so that a reader who
prefers that pair need recompute nothing. @sec-digits says how many of the
printed decimal places the simulation supports.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coef-full
#| tbl-cap: "The 21 landscape slopes in full, each with the decision it supports beside the estimate, the interval and the ROPE mass that decision rests on. `median`, `2.5%`, `97.5%` are on the link scale; `std` columns divide by the link-scale SD of the response, which is the axis the 0.1 ROPE is defined on; `response scale` translates the median to a percentage change per unit of the predictor (log and logit links) or leaves it in the response's own units (identity link). 'Direction certainty' is max(P(beta > 0), P(beta < 0)): 0.5 means the posterior is split evenly about zero, 1.0 that the sign is certain. The last column is the smallest ROPE half-width at which the 95% interval would have fitted entirely inside, in the response's own units (@sec-min-rope)."
cf |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor), Link,
            median = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            mode = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `std median` = Std_median, `std 2.5%` = Std_lo, `std 97.5%` = Std_hi,
            `% in ROPE` = fmt(pct_in_ROPE, 1),
            `direction certainty` = fmt(Dir_certainty, 3),
            Decision = Verdict,
            `response scale [95% ETI]` = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]",
              fmt(Resp_median, 1), fmt(Resp_lo, 1), fmt(Resp_hi, 1)),
            unit = Min_ROPE_unit,
            `min ROPE, response scale` = sprintf("+/- %s %s",
              fmt(abs(Min_ROPE_resp), 1), Min_ROPE_unit)) |>
  kt(caption = NULL, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-post
#| fig-cap: "Prior (grey) against posterior (blue) for every slope, on the standardised axis. The shaded band is the ROPE. Where the two curves nearly coincide, the data have said little."
SHOW("prior_posterior.png")
```

## Locality-Level Variance and Correlation Structure {#sec-icc}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 3.B, for the parameters that answer Q1.
:::

The intraclass correlation is
$\mathrm{ICC}^{(r)} = \sigma_u^{(r)2} / (\sigma_u^{(r)2} + \sigma_{\text{resid}}^{(r)2})$,
computed **draw by draw** so that it acquires a full posterior. The residual
variance is taken on the link scale, and its form depends on the family:
$\sigma^2$ for the gaussian and lognormal responses;
$\log(1 + 1/\mu + 1/\text{shape})$ evaluated at the intercept for the
negative binomial; and, for the two zero-one-inflated beta responses,
$\psi'(\mu\phi) + \psi'((1-\mu)\phi)$, the logit-scale variance of the beta
component. For those two the ICC therefore describes the beta component alone
and ignores the inflation (@sec-likelihood).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc
icc_ref |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Family = unname(fam_lab[Family]),
            `locality SD` = sd_median, `SD 2.5%` = sd_lo, `SD 97.5%` = sd_hi,
            `ICC median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `ICC mode` = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `P(ICC > 0.05)` = P_gt_rope, Rhat = rhat,
            `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk), Verdict) |>
  arrange(desc(`ICC median`)) |>
  kt(caption = "Locality SD and intraclass correlation, with diagnostics for the derived quantity.", digits = 3)
```

## The 21 Locality-Intercept Correlations {#sec-cor}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.B and 3.B. These 21 parameters are part of the model and no
research question is about them, so they are reported here in full rather than
in the main narrative.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-cor
#| fig-cap: "Posterior median of each of the 21 locality-intercept correlations. Bold entries are those whose 95% equal-tailed interval excludes zero."
SHOW("correlation_matrix.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cor
cor_tb |>
  transmute(`Response A` = rlab(A), `Response B` = rlab(B),
            median = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            mode = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `P(rho > 0)` = P_positive, Rhat = rhat, `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(median))) |>
  kt(caption = "All 21 correlations among the locality intercepts, ordered by absolute posterior median. With 26 clusters these are weakly identified; the LKJ(1) prior is uniform over correlation matrices and S5 varies it.", digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-caterpillar
#| fig-cap: "Locality offsets on the link scale, one panel per response, with 95% equal-tailed intervals. Localities are in one fixed order in every panel, largest assemblage first, with the specimen count in brackets. Reading down each panel shows partial pooling at work: the smaller the assemblage, the harder the offset is pulled towards zero and the wider its interval."
SHOW("locality_intercepts.png")
```

# Appendix F. Sensitivity Analysis in Full {#sec-sensitivity}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.
:::

Seven fits, identical in every respect except the prior, each changing one
element of the reference specification. A full factorial would have made any
movement impossible to attribute, so the design here changes one thing at a
time (@sec-model-series). S1 is the unscaled `normal(0, 1)` slope prior
discussed in @sec-priors, which is also the specification `paper/_analysis.R`
uses for the main paper's summary tables (@sec-reproducibility).

S6 differs in kind from the rest. S1 to S5 vary how much the data are allowed
to say about a quantity the report decides on; S6 removes a parameter the data
cannot inform, so its curves in @fig-sens-icc and @fig-sens-slopes coincide
with the reference by construction (@sec-oneinflated).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-specs
kt(data.frame(
  Fit = c("REF", names(prior_specs)[-1]),
  `Prior change` = c(prior_specs$REF$label,
                     sapply(prior_specs[-1], function(x) x$label)),
  Rationale = c(prior_specs$REF$note, sapply(prior_specs[-1], function(x) x$note)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL),
  caption = "The seven prior specifications. REF is the reference; each of S1 to S6 changes exactly one line of it.")
```

## Broad Prior {#sec-5a}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.A.
:::

S2 widens every slope prior by a factor of 2.5, to
`normal(0, 2.5 x SD_link)`. This is the broad prior the guideline asks for: if
the posterior barely moves when the prior becomes two and a half times more
permissive, the result rests on the data instead of on the prior. S3 and S4
play the same role for the locality SD, and S5 for the correlation matrix.

## Variations of the Default Priors {#sec-5c}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.C.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens-icc
#| fig-cap: "Q1 under all seven priors: the cumulative posterior distribution of each ICC. The shaded band is the ICC ROPE [0, 0.05]. A curve's height where it crosses the right edge of the band is P(ICC <= 0.05)."
SHOW("sensitivity_icc.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens-slopes
#| fig-cap: "Q2 under all seven priors, for the slopes most exposed to the prior: the three edge-angle slopes (the response that was prior-dominated under the original specification) and the height slope of every response. Cumulative distributions on the standardised axis, with the ROPE shaded."
SHOW("sensitivity_slopes.png")
```

The curves are cumulative distributions rather than densities, because this
report's summaries are quantiles: a horizontal slice at 0.025 and 0.975 reads
off the interval limits directly, and the vertical distance between two curves
at the ROPE edge is the change in the quantity the decision rule uses.

BARG asks for the numbers as well as the pictures, and for every parameter
rather than only the plotted ones:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-full
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior median and 95% equal-tailed interval for every ICC and every slope, under each of the seven priors. Slopes are standardised by the link-scale SD of their response."
sens_long |>
  mutate(cell = ci(Median, lo, hi, 2)) |>
  select(Quantity, Spec, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Spec, values_from = cell) |>
  kt(caption = NULL)
```

## Do the Conclusions Change? {#sec-5e}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.E. Some movement is inevitable, so the criterion is whether
the numbers moved enough, relative to the width of the posterior interval and
relative to the ROPE, to change a conclusion.
:::

@sec-prior-dependence gives the summary and quotes the largest movement of a
posterior median across the seven priors. The table here gives the detail
behind the decisions: what each quantity is judged to be under each prior.
@tbl-sens-full above supplies the estimates those judgements come from.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-verdict
kt(changed |> select(-n_distinct_dec),
   caption = "The decision each quantity receives under each prior.")
```

# Appendix G. BARG Conformance {#sec-barg}

Kruschke (2021) sets out a checklist for reporting a Bayesian analysis. The
table below places every item on it against the section that answers it. The
same checklist can be walked from the other direction: each section of this
document opens with a shaded box naming the item it addresses.

This table sits at the end rather than at the front because the narrative of
this document follows the order of the work rather than the order of the
checklist (@sec-summary). A reader auditing coverage should start here; a
reader following the argument will have passed every row already.

| BARG item | How it is addressed | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Preamble A.** Why a Bayesian approach is used | Seven responses on three link scales share one locality-level structure in a single model; derived quantities acquire genuine intervals; a null value can be accepted rather than merely not rejected; no large-sample approximation is needed in a design with few clusters | @sec-why-bayes |
| **Preamble B.** The goals of the analysis | Estimation of each landscape effect and of the locality variance, and decisions about null values. Prediction and model comparison are not goals | @sec-goals |
| **1.A.** Data variables, their roles and types | Seven responses, three locality-level predictors, one grouping factor, with the observed range of each; the complete-case filter is audited step by step; the estimand and the design that produced the sample are stated separately | @sec-design, @sec-data, @tbl-data-vars, @tbl-dropped |
| **1.B.** The likelihood and its parameters, separating those of theoretical interest from nuisance parameters | One multivariate model over four distributional families, with the linear predictor written out; the slopes and the locality SDs answer the questions, the intercepts, dispersion parameters and 21 correlations do not | @sec-likelihood, @tbl-likelihood |
| **1.C.** The prior distribution and its justification | Every class given an explicit prior, the slope prior scaled to each response's own link-scale SD, with the share of prior mass inside each response's ROPE as the argument for scaling it | @sec-priors, @sec-priors-full |
| **1.D.** Formal specification of the model | model formula / Stan code available from the analysis code or archive | analysis code or archive |
| **1.E.** Prior predictive check | The reference prior refitted with `sample_prior = "only"`, and the simulated data checked against the physically possible range of each measure | @sec-prior-pred, @tbl-prior-pred |
| **2.A.** Software, versions and settings | R, brms, backend and CmdStan versions, chains, iterations, warmup, seed, `adapt_delta` and `max_treedepth`, for all eleven runs | @sec-software, @tbl-software |
| **2.B.** MCMC chain convergence | R-hat, divergent transitions and treedepth saturation, for the reference fit and for all eleven runs, with rank plots of the chains behind the reference fit | @sec-convergence, @tbl-diag-all, @fig-mcmc-rank |
| **2.C.** MCMC chain resolution | Bulk and tail effective sample size for every parameter and every derived ICC, plotted in @fig-convergence and tabulated with the Monte Carlo standard error of each quantile the report quotes; the locality offsets and correlations omitted from the printed table are in the archive; an audit of how many decimal places that error supports | @sec-resolution, @sec-digits, @tbl-convergence, @fig-convergence |
| **2.D.** Accuracy of any approximation used in place of exact sampling | Not applicable: every posterior in this document is a full MCMC sample, with no variational, Laplace or INLA approximation anywhere | Not applicable |
| **3.A.** Posterior predictive check | Full predictive distributions, a check of the within-basin medians, and test statistics fixed in advance | @sec-post-pred, @sec-ppc-stats, @tbl-ppc-stats |
| **3.B.** Summary of the posterior of every parameter | Posterior median and 95% equal-tailed interval, with mode and 95% HDI alongside, for the 21 slopes, the seven locality SDs and ICCs, and the 21 correlations | @sec-posterior-summary, @sec-icc, @sec-cor |
| **3.C.** Bayes factors and posterior model probabilities | Not applicable: no model comparison is performed, so no marginal likelihood, no bridge sampling and no Bayes factor appears anywhere in this document | Not applicable (@sec-goals) |
| **4.A.** The decision procedure and its rule | Kruschke's (2018) three-way decision (reject, accept, undecided) against a region of practical equivalence | @sec-decision-rule |
| **4.B.** The loss or utility function, where decisions are made by formal decision theory | Not applicable: no cost attaches to being wrong about a landscape slope, so no loss function is specified; the ROPE curve reports the whole family of decisions instead of committing to one | Not applicable (@sec-rope) |
| **4.C.** ROPE limits and their justification | Half-width 0.1 of each response's link-scale SD, with the convention acknowledged and the posterior mass reported as a continuous function of the half-width | @sec-rope, @fig-rope |
| **4.D.** Bayes-factor decision thresholds | Not applicable: no Bayes factor is used, so no threshold on one is needed | Not applicable (@sec-goals) |
| **4.E.** Each decision reported with the estimate and interval it rests on | Every decision table gives the median, the 95% interval, the posterior mass inside the ROPE and the verdict in the same row | @sec-q1, @sec-q2 |
| **5.A.** Sensitivity to a broad prior | S2 widens every slope prior by a factor of 2.5; S3, S4 and S5 do the same job for the locality SD and for the correlation matrix | @sec-5a, @tbl-sens-specs |
| **5.B.** Sensitivity to a genuinely informed prior drawn from previous research | Not applicable: no published posterior or meta-analytic estimate exists for any of these seven measures in Quina assemblages, so no informed prior can be built; the gap is discussed where the priors are set out | Not applicable (@sec-priors) |
| **5.C.** Variations of the default priors | Six fits, each differing from the reference in exactly one prior, with every ICC and every slope reported under all seven specifications; the eleven fits and the purpose of each are set out together | @sec-model-series, @sec-5c, @tbl-sens-full |
| **5.D.** Sensitivity of the Bayes factor to the prior | Not applicable: no Bayes factor is computed. The item is singled out in the guideline because Bayes factors are prior-dependent in a way posterior estimates are not, which is part of why this analysis is framed as estimation | Not applicable (@sec-goals) |
| **5.E.** Whether the conclusions change | The decision each quantity receives under each of the seven priors, and the largest movement of a posterior median relative to that quantity's own interval width; and, for the one structural question the design can pose, whether the landscape slopes differ between the two basins | @sec-prior-dependence, @sec-basinx, @sec-5e |
| **6.** Reproducibility of data, code and computational environment | Software versions, the file list, the archive DOI, a synthetic dataset for the case where the specimens cannot be released, run instructions and `sessionInfo()` | @sec-reproducibility |


## What the Checklist Does Not Ask For

Three parts of this document answer to the second standard rather than to this
one, and a reader auditing BARG coverage will not find rows for them.
@sec-design states the estimand and the design before any model appears, so
that the resolution of both research questions is fixed in the open rather
than inferred from wide intervals later. @sec-model-series sets out all eleven
fits together with the reason each exists, including the two that record a
defect the analysis found in itself. @sec-sbc says which computational check
this report has not performed, why, and what a follow-up should do instead.
None of the three is required by Kruschke (2021), and each is standard in
Gelman, Vehtari, McElreath, et al. (2026).
